rows.subtype: Approach: root-cause thinking about how data was shared so freely [Thinking]
rows.description: Asking why so many services had the same details, the person decides to give minimum data, use a separate email for sign-ups and read permissions. Tracing the cause changes future habits.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: avoidance and procrastination, forward planning

rows.subtype: Approach: alert friends and family to expect phishing [Action]
rows.description: Since contact lists were part of the leak, the person tells relatives to ignore suspicious messages asking for money or OTPs. Warning others reduces spread of harm.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: avoidance and procrastination, forward planning

rows.subtype: Approach: assume nothing is at risk because nothing was stolen [Pitfall]
rows.description: The person reasons that only an email address leaked and dismisses the risk. Combined with other data, the address later enables targeted scams, showing how small leaks add up.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: avoidance and procrastination, forward planning

rows.subtype: Approach: decide which tasks the tool should and should not do [Thinking]
rows.description: A final-year student sets a rule that AI can explain concepts and check grammar, but cannot write the submitted analysis. Choosing the purpose first keeps the tool as an aid to learning.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: critical path, impulsive action, negotiation

rows.subtype: Approach: verify AI outputs against reliable sources [Action]
rows.description: Before using a summary of a paper, the person checks the claims and citations in the original source. Verification is needed because tools can produce confident but wrong statements.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: critical path, impulsive action, negotiation

rows.subtype: Approach: paste the assignment and submit the result [Pitfall]
rows.description: Pressed for time, a student submits an AI-written essay unchanged. The work has errors, breaks the institution's policy on originality and teaches nothing, so the shortcut costs more later.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: critical path, impulsive action, negotiation

rows.subtype: Approach: read the institution and employer AI policy first [Action]
rows.description: The employee checks the company guideline before pasting client documents into a public chatbot, and asks the manager about approved tools. Confidential data should not be entered into unapproved services.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: critical path, impulsive action, negotiation

rows.subtype: Approach: use the tool as a tutor with own attempt first [Thinking]
rows.description: The student attempts a coding problem, then asks the tool to explain the error and quiz them on the concept. Trying first keeps thinking active and makes the help stick.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: critical path, impulsive action, negotiation

rows.subtype: Approach: trust the output because it sounds fluent [Pitfall]
rows.description: A young analyst uses a tool-generated figure in a report without checking it. A manager finds the number invented, which harms credibility. Fluency is mistaken for accuracy.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: critical path, negotiation

rows.subtype: Approach: add disclosure and keep a record of use [Revision]
rows.description: After a professor's question, the student begins noting where AI helped and includes an acknowledgment in submitted work. Adjusting to openness protects trust and clarifies what is their own work.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: critical path, impulsive action, negotiation
